detail: Live on HEAD 3956cfb: initialize + tools/list via 4-byte BE length-prefixed framing (the MCP spec stdio transport, what real MCP clients use) → no response in 5s, process stays alive; same requests newline-delimited with stdin held open → both respond immediately (13 tools). The report's 'stdin-open hang' is the wrong mechanism — framing is the blocker; EOF-piped and newline-delimited stdin-open both work.
foreman_note: Measured with bin/crier-mcp built from d337b3f: a 4-byte big-endian length-prefixed initialize frame gets an immediate JSON-RPC response {"jsonrpc":"2.0","error":{"code":-32700,"message":"parse error"},"id":null} and the process exits 0 with stdin closed — not the 'no response in 5s, process stays alive' the row states. The silence it saw is NDJSON waiting for a line terminator while stdin is held open with no newline; newline-delimited framing IS the MCP stdio transport framing, so crier is spec-conformant. A future docs tick may add one line to README saying so, but there is no defect to fix.

detail: Deep-debug audit 2026-09-14: the two hottest events on a message bus — a relay publish accepted and a webhook delivery dispatched — emit ZERO log lines (internal/relay/handler.go: 0 slog calls; internal/webhook/driver.go: 0). detail: Worker out-of-scope finding during DF-CRIER-151 (worker c319e6f, live postgres probe /tmp/crier-t268/probe-out.txt): the PATCH /agents/{id} response echoes the PRE-write last_seen. Step 5 (the PATCH, HTTP 200) returns last_seen=2026-09-14T23:19:17.600589-05:00 while step 6 (GET immediately after) returns 2026-09-14T23:19:20.31042-05:00, i.e. the response body is rendered from the caller's in-memory copy rather than from the row that was just written. The in-memory backend is further behind: it never advances last_seen at all on update (Update writes capabilities/webhook/guard only), so a client cannot use last_seen from a PATCH response to confirm the write. No data is lost and delivery is unaffected — this is a wire-contract inconsistency, not the DF-CRIER-151 failure shape. Fix direction: have both stores refresh agent.LastSeen (and the other persisted defaults) on the caller's object before the handler renders the response, with a test asserting the PATCH response's last_seen equals the subsequent GET's.

detail: CI run 35038607923 (push of board commit 3c0242c) failed Build & Test on internal/registry: TestDeliver_Blocking_TimeoutIs504/endpoint_hangs_past_the_budget got status=200 body={"id":"...","transport":"webhook","reply":""} instead of the expected 504. The endpoint sleeps 2s, budget is 100ms, so the first attempt should time out and DeliverBlocking should return the 'timed out' error -> 504. A 200 with an empty reply means c.http.Do returned a completed (empty-body) 2xx within the budget, i.e. the client's http.Client.Timeout cut the hanging attempt even though cfg.TimeoutMs=100 was far below the next retry's needs. Foreman repro: passes -count=8 (residue), then 20/20 isolated subtest and 30/30 full-package after go clean -testcache (58/58 total) on this host. Code read: webhook.Client has a DRIVER-GLOBAL timeout (NewClient(timeout, secret)); the blocking attempt request carries NO per-attempt context deadline (postBody builds without ctx), so per-attempt waits rely on the global client timeout only; handler.go:590 maps req.TimeoutMs->budget=100ms correctly. Also verify whether deliverHarness's TimeoutMs:100 override reaches the client (webhook.Config.TimeoutMs) or only sets the budget. Fix candidates: (a) give the blocking attempt context.WithTimeout(remaining budget) so an attempt can never overrun the budget; (b) harden the test (longer hang, wall-clock assert); (c) check no package-level shared webhook.Client with a short timeout bleeds across tests in the same package. Evidence trail: tick 271 audit event 451; gh run 35038607923 failed-step log; internal/webhook/driver.go DeliverBlocking; internal/webhook/webhook.go postBody; internal/registry/handler.go:590.

reasoning.note: foreman tick 271 — post-push CI red on a push carrying ZERO code touching this path; local clean-cache 58/58 green; real race candidate filed per CI-health mandate

review_notes: Root cause was NOT the filed hypothesis (a client timeout cutting a hanging attempt): the attempt was unbounded by the caller's budget and the test's 2s endpoint sleep photo-finished the harness's driver-global 2s http.Client.Timeout, so a loaded run accepted a 200-empty-reply as success. Fix is in the production path (no test was weakened). Semantics preserved: ctx deadline stays Retryable -> 504, non-retryable rejections and unmappable 2xx stay ErrPermanent -> 502.
title: [CI:P2] TestDeliver_Blocking_TimeoutIs504/endpoint_hangs_past_the_budget flaked red on tick-271 board push (run 35038607923) — 200+empty reply instead of 504; passes 58/58 clean-cache reruns locally; client timeout is driver-global not per-attempt
worker_summary: DeliverBlocking now bounds each ATTEMPT by the remaining budget: remaining := time.Until(deadline) (clamped to 1ns when <=0) is passed to a new Client.PostContext via context.WithTimeout, and postBody builds the request with http.NewRequestWithContext. Before this change the attempt was bounded only by the driver-global http.Client.Timeout fixed at NewClient(timeout, secret) - Config.TimeoutMs never reached the client - so a delivery with timeout_ms=100 could run for the full global timeout and, when the endpoint's late 2xx won the race, be reported to the caller as a SUCCESS. Post/PostBatch keep their signatures and delegate with context.Background() (no caller churn). Deterministic regression test TestDeliverBlocking_AttemptBoundedByRemainingBudget (2s endpoint, 10s global client timeout, 100ms budget) FAILS on the pre-fix driver with 'err = nil, reply = late-reply after 2.002s - an over-budget endpoint 2xx was reported as a SUCCESS' and PASSES after. Previously red shape green 3x consecutively (13/13 packages), TestDeliver_Blocking_TimeoutIs504 -count=10 ok; judge PASS 2c095725.

detail: internal/registry/remote.go:245-255 List swallows EVERY decode error: `if err := s.do(http.MethodGet, "/agents", nil, &out); err != nil { return []*Agent{} }`. A decode failure, a 401/403 and a 5xx are therefore all indistinguishable from an EMPTY REGISTRY on the bridge surface, and the failure is silent (no log, no error returned to the caller). DF-CRIER-198 (c4f2f04) removed the one trigger that existed at the time - a keyless agent whose empty public_key failed HexKey.UnmarshalJSON - by making the decode accept the empty key; the pattern that turned that decode failure into a confident zero-agent answer is untouched, so the NEXT decode regression (schema drift on Agent, a new field, a changed wire shape) will be reported to an MCP bridge as `{"agents":[]}` instead of as an error. Reproduce at c4f2f04: point a RemoteStore at a server that answers /agents with a shape it cannot decode (or with a 500) and observe List() returning an empty slice with no error and no log line. Acceptance: RemoteStore.List stops laundering failures into an empty slice - either the decode error is surfaced to the caller (an error return, or a distinguishable sentinel) or it is at minimum logged once per occurrence with the status/body context, while a genuinely empty registry still returns an empty slice; an erroring server must be distinguishable from an empty one by a bridge caller, and focused tests cover both the empty-registry case and the undecodable-response case. Filed from the DF-CRIER-198 worker's out-of-scope report; premise re-verified by the foreman at c4f2f04 by reading remote.go:245-255.

detail: Measured on this tick's own commits. adb77da (QA-CRIER-9: scripts/lib/port-guard.sh + two run-demo.sh + Makefile + ci.yml + two .md) and its gitreins record 8205035 both passed the pre-commit hook with the line 'No supported source files found. Supported extensions: go, py, ts, tsx, ...' while the guard summary still read 'Tier 1 Guards: PASS (test mode: full)'. The guard filters staged files by extension, so a diff with no supported source file short-circuits and the PASS means 'nothing was checked', not 'nothing is wrong'. Consequence: shell scripts, Makefile recipes and CI workflow YAML can land with zero gate evidence, and a tick that trusts the hook green is trusting a vacuous result (this tick had to run go build/vet/test, make docs-check and the new selftest by hand to get real evidence). Fix direction: run shellcheck on staged .sh files and a YAML parse on .github/workflows/*.yml, or at minimum print an explicit non-vacuity line ('no guardable files staged - nothing verified') and make the tier-1 verdict distinguishable from a real pass, so a green cannot be manufactured.

The captured 'output' the classifier judged is the image sha256 line — the real signature ('deadline_exceeded', 'stream error') was on the line just before it, i.e. the classifier is reading the wrong line (or the wrong stream) of a multi-line attempt, so any cell deploy whose failure text is a stream error is unretryable. This is a follow-on to INT-CI-001 (commit 65aa127), which added exactly this retry+classify leg for the ssh/scp reset case and is complete — the classifier's signature set is what is incomplete, not the retry loop. title: [P2] Stale-pidfile takeover window: a failed-bind start exits silently while the old pidfile stays plausible, and `kill $(cat .crier.pid)` breaks on the JSON shape — found by dogfood 2026-09-24.
detail: FOUND BY DOGFOOD 2026-09-24 on the ephemeral bunker (las-bunker-03, agent 9ef9da05, clean Debian 13, non-root, HEAD ca28523). Live sequence: (1) server running with pidfile .crier.pid (JSON: {"pid":3917949,...}); (2) a second `./bin/crier -port 8767` start fails to bind and exits with level=ERROR 'server failed: another process already holds this port' naming the holder and hinting correctly; (3) the OLD process keeps serving; (4) the pidfile on disk still describes the old server, so a user who believes their restart happened reads a plausible pidfile that does not describe the world they think they are in. Two concrete edges: (a) `kill $(cat .crier.pid)` — the first thing any user tries — fails with bash 'kill: {: arguments must be process or job IDs' because the pidfile is JSON, and nothing in `make stop`'s docs mentions that (make stop itself works); (b) nothing warns at failed-bind time that an EXISTING pidfile describes a different (or dead) process — the one moment a user is confused about which server is answering is exactly the moment crier has the information to say so. ASK: at failed-bind time, when a pidfile exists, log one line explaining what the pidfile names (pid X — still running and holding the port / dead since ...) and how to stop it (make stop); and either make `make stop`'s error path document the JSON pidfile shape, or write a bare-pid first line so `kill $(cat .crier.pid)` works. Evidence commands in docs/dogfood/2026-09-24-real-use.md.

detail: A2A is task-oriented: Task with TaskState, and GetTask (GET /tasks/{id}), ListTasks (GET /tasks), CancelTask (POST /tasks/{id}:cancel), SubscribeToTask (POST /tasks/{id}:subscribe). DELIVERABLE: map a crier inbox entry onto an A2A Task WITHOUT inventing a second store — an undelivered message is a submitted/working task, a leased message is working, an acked message is TASK_STATE_COMPLETED, a TTL-expired message is TASK_STATE_FAILED (documented choice), and a cancel request releases the lease and closes the entry (crier already has ack/release semantics; reuse them). title: [P1] Mesh carries NO authentication — identity is the URL path only, so any network-reachable client can impersonate an agent on the lateral-movement lane (external review #1).
detail: Carter's #1 finding, VERIFIED at HEAD 0b60acc: `grep -rnE 'requireAgent|Signature|token|auth' internal/mesh/*.go` returns ZERO hits. `/mesh/connect/{agentID}` proves nothing about the caller — the agent id is a PATH CLAIM, not an identity — while crier's registry holds an ed25519 key per agent and enforces it on the inbox lane. Net effect: the one lane built for agent-to-agent request/response is the one lane where a compromised or hostile peer can speak as anyone, and the review reports the origin policy is allow-all by default. HONEST FRAMING: this is documented-by-design in docs/mesh-protocol.md, not a silent defect — but it is the biggest verified hole for any multi-agent or shared deployment, because it bypasses the identity story crier advertises. ACCEPTANCE (one of, chosen in the spec): an ed25519 challenge on connect, per-frame signatures, or a session token issued at connect and required on frames; PLUS the origin policy made explicit and configurable rather than allow-all. Do NOT silently tighten the default in a way that breaks existing single-host deployments — ship it behind the documented config with a migration note. Evidence owed: a frame from an unauthenticated peer rejected, and an authenticated one accepted, captured live. SOURCE: external hands-on review 'DISPATCH · CRI-001' by Carter (delivered 2026-09-25 via Bane), tested live at ca28523d on 2026-09-24 on a scratch port with the guard disabled per TESTERS.md §1. Claims below were re-verified at HEAD 0b60acc before filing — re-measure, don't transcribe. Credit the reporter in the closing commit.
worker_summary: Mesh connect admits a peer only after an opt-in ed25519 challenge (CR_REQUIRE_MESH_AUTH, DEFAULT FALSE = measured no change) and a mesh-only CR_MESH_ALLOWED_ORIGINS policy; on an authenticated mesh a REQUEST whose source.agent_id is not the proven peer is refused FORBIDDEN and replies bind to the addressed peer; GET /status reports mesh_auth_required and mesh_origin_policy. title: [P2] The durable lane cannot tap an agent's shoulder: inbox long-poll (?wait_seconds) + a new-message ping.
detail: VERIFIED at HEAD: internal/registry/handler.go takes limit/lease_seconds only — there is no wait/block/long-poll parameter anywhere, so the inbox is strictly poll-only. The review states the consequence well: the one lane that promises DURABILITY is the one lane that cannot wake a sleeping agent, so a 60s poll loop learns about urgent work up to a minute late and a rarely-polling agent may as well be offline. DELIVERABLE: (1) `?wait_seconds=` on GET /agents/{id}/inbox (bounded, default 0 = today's behaviour) that returns as soon as a message is available or the budget expires with an empty set — the long-poll every agent framework already understands; (2) a lightweight new-message ping for agents that cannot hold a connection (webhook-style POST, or a tick on the existing mesh socket). MUST NOT change existing semantics: absent/0 wait_seconds must be byte-identical to today, and lease/ack/TTL behaviour is untouched. ACCEPTANCE: a long-poll returns early on delivery, times out empty correctly, and the poll-only path is unchanged; a test proves the pre-existing no-wait response is identical. SOURCE: external hands-on review 'DISPATCH · CRI-001' by Carter (delivered 2026-09-25 via Bane), tested live at ca28523d on 2026-09-24 on a scratch port with the guard disabled per TESTERS.md §1. Claims below were re-verified at HEAD 0b60acc before filing — re-measure, don't transcribe. Credit the reporter in the closing commit.
worker_summary: Inbox long-poll (?wait_seconds=0..120, default 0) parks a retrieve until a message is claimable or the budget expires (expiry answers the byte-identical poll-only empty body); a delivery signals the agent's parked reads (subscribe-before-read, no lost wakeup); a per-connection ?inbox_notify=1 opts into a server->agent INBOX_NOTIFY ping on the existing mesh socket. Additive: absent/0 wait is byte-identical, lease/ack/TTL untouched — TestInboxPollOnlyPathIsUnchanged pins it.

title: [P2] Make presence true: mesh heartbeats should feed registry last_seen/status (crashed agents currently report 'online').
detail: The review calls liveness 'a known lie': crashed agents still show status online with frozen last_seen, and it calls any dashboard built on GET /agents today actively misleading. VERIFIED: the mesh peer loop DOES tick and send TypeKeepalive and peer.go handles the case (peer.go:231/238/291), but that traffic does not advance the registry row — the dogfood lane independently confirmed status is registration-only and last_seen advances only on a signed PATCH. So the signal already flows and is simply not wired to the thing that reports liveness. DELIVERABLE: heartbeats (or signed PATCHes) advance last_seen, and status derives from a documented staleness window so a dead agent goes stale instead of staying online forever; the README's honest note stays, but says what makes a row stale rather than that liveness is unavailable. ACCEPTANCE: kill an agent mid-session and the registry row goes stale within the documented window, with the transition captured live. Prerequisite for operating any fleet past a handful of agents. title: [P2] Finish task ownership: sender idempotency keys, a dead-letter queue, TTL-expiry receipts, and transfer/reassign.
detail: The review's 'the lease is the lock' section is right and VERIFIED: `grep -i idempot internal/` finds only Start/Stop comments — there is NO sender-supplied idempotency key, so a retried deliver duplicates work; TTL expiry purges silently with no notify path, so a sender never learns its work died; there is no transfer/reassign and no DLQ (only webhook BATCHES dead-letter on permanent 4xx — a precedent to copy, not a general mechanism). DELIVERABLE: (1) optional `idempotency_key` on deliver, deduplicating within a documented window; (2) an expiry/unacked receipt to the sender (the existing FEDERATION_FAILED / WEBHOOK_FAILED pattern is the house style for 'failure is a message, not a mystery'); (3) a dead-letter destination for messages that expire unacked; (4) reassign/transfer so a foreman can rebalance a stuck lease. ACCEPTANCE: a duplicated idempotent deliver yields one message; an expired message produces exactly one receipt; a dead-lettered message is retrievable from the DLQ path. This is the Celery-visibility-timeout / Temporal playbook ported — do it in the existing lease model, not beside it. SOURCE: external hands-on review 'DISPATCH · CRI-001' by Carter (delivered 2026-09-25 via Bane), tested live at ca28523d on 2026-09-24 on a scratch port with the guard disabled per TESTERS.md §1. Claims below were re-verified at HEAD 0b60acc before filing — re-measure, don't transcribe. Credit the reporter in the closing commit.

title: [P2] Kill the signing ceremony: `crier keygen` plus first-party Python/TS clients (the review's named number-one adoption killer).
detail: The review is blunt and correct: registering an agent means OpenSSL 3 + xxd key surgery + a hand-written sig() shell helper, and that ceremony is the top adoption killer — it is also what the last three external/first-party testers each tripped over (Bharat's report, the dogfood xxd trap DF-CRIER-280, and this review). PARTLY ALREADY FIXED, and say so in the closing note: the SPECIFIC misleading failure the review cites — a piped payload silently producing an empty signature and a 401 blaming the headers — was fixed under DF-CRIER-236 (a4a4619, the 401 now names an empty/malformed signature) and the one-shot pkeyutl trap is documented in the README. The CEREMONY itself remains. DELIVERABLE: (1) `crier keygen` producing a keypair + printed agent config with no openssl incantation; (2) thin Python and TypeScript clients that sign for you (register/deliver/retrieve/ack/publish/subscribe as methods, not curl recipes). ACCEPTANCE: a tester with no crypto background registers and completes a signed round-trip using only the CLI and a client library, start to finish, transcript attached. SOURCE: external hands-on review 'DISPATCH · CRI-001' by Carter (delivered 2026-09-25 via Bane), tested live at ca28523d on 2026-09-24 on a scratch port with the guard disabled per TESTERS.md §1. title: [P2] Detection, not just attribution — the Hugging Face lesson: signed delivery log, behaviour baselines, kill-switch, canary tokens.
detail: The sharpest analysis in the review, and it lands on a real gap: asked whether crier could have seen the July-2026 agent-intrusion incident coming, the honest answer is that it would have ATTRIBUTED the attack afterwards, never DETECTED it during. VERIFIED absences at HEAD: no append-only delivery log, no behaviour baselines or anomaly signal, no kill-switch, no canary tokens (grep for delivery_log/dead-letter/canary/kill-switch finds only a webhook batch test). Crier already holds the three pieces detection needs — ed25519 attribution, a guard choke point, and failure receipts — so this is wiring, not invention. DELIVERABLE, ranked: (1) an append-only, signed delivery log (who sent what to whom, when, and the verdict) that survives restarts; (2) baseline signals with alerts on fan-out spikes, new-peer bursts and odd-hour volume; (3) a single-call kill-switch (unregister + revoke leases + pause webhooks + quarantine the agent); (4) canary tokens an exfiltrating agent trips over. ACCEPTANCE: a scripted 'compromised agent' that fans out to N new peers trips a documented alert and is contained by the kill-switch in one call, captured live. This is the item that turns crier from a bus into something an operator can run on a network with adversaries on it. title: [P2] Chaos-verify the two lanes the reviewer refused to trust: federation partitions (hold/retry/recovery) and the guard's fail-closed mode.

That is the correct instinct: federation carries an explicit failure semantic (FEDERATION_FAILED receipts, hold queue, first-non-404-wins, CR_FED_MAX_HOLD_S, CR_FED_QUEUE_FILE) that has never been exercised under an actual partition in a committed test. DELIVERABLE: a committed chaos cell in scripts/e2e-battery.sh that (a) stands up two linked relays, partitions the link mid-flight, and asserts the documented semantics — the delivery is held (202 held), retried on recovery, and a terminal failure produces exactly ONE FEDERATION_FAILED receipt to the sender rather than a silent drop; (b) drives the guard with its provider deliberately unavailable and asserts the DOCUMENTED fail-closed decision for each policy, proving the failure mode is the chosen one and not an accident. Both cells must FAIL CLOSED: if the link cannot be established at all, the cell is an error, never a pass. title: [P3] Priority lanes and real backpressure — beyond a per-agent 100/min cap, with queue depth visible.
detail: Two related gaps the review names in passing but which matter at any real load: 'no priority lanes' (in the task-ownership section) and 'the 100/min/agent cap is the only backpressure'. Today a steady stream of low-value messages can starve an urgent one, and nothing sheds load globally — a single runaway producer either gets 429ed per-agent or pushes the queue deeper with no visibility. DELIVERABLE: (a) a message priority (documented field, default = today's behaviour, higher retrieved first within an agent's inbox); (b) a global (and, once CR-FEAT-029 namespaces land, per-namespace) rate limit that sheds with a NAMED error — the review notes the 429 carries no Retry-After header, so add one — instead of growing unbounded; (c) queue depth surfaced where operators already look (/status, /metrics). WHAT HAPPENED (measured, not inferred): CI runs `go test -short -count=1 ./...`.
TestCRFEAT029NamespaceDocumentCanComeFromAFile failed DETERMINISTICALLY on two
consecutive CI runs (CI 36207787751 and 36207783512, both "server did not start

CI's exact flags (`go test -short -count=1 ./cmd/server` -> ok, 26.5s).

TWO FACTS PINNED THE CAUSE:
1. the port the test polled (`:44695`, `:36501`) NEVER appears in a "crier
   starting port=" line in either CI log - so the server did not fail to bind it;
2. after raising the budget to 20s, CI went GREEN (CI 36208294847, all four jobs)

   returning an error, the in-process server was simply SLOWER than 10s to

IN-PROCESS and polls /health with a fixed 10s deadline. On CI, cmd/server's
suite runs beside every other package's test binary, and that deadline is too
tight. It is not a product bug and not a port race.

answering /health" diagnostic that names the port, so the next failure of this
class says WHY instead of timing out silently).
